chapter.title: React in depth
chapter.summary: How React actually renders, reconciles and memoises, how Server Components and Server Actions split work across the network, and how concurrent features keep the UI responsive.

lessons.title: The React rendering model
lessons.summary: Render vs commit, why components re-render, reconciliation on fibers, keys and state identity, automatic batching, memoisation and what the React Compiler does and does not fix.

parts.label: Render, commit, keys
parts.body:
## The mental model in one paragraph React is a function from state to UI that runs again whenever state changes. "Rendering" in React does **not** mean touching the DOM. It means calling your component functions to get a description of what the UI should look like. React then compares that description with the previous one and, in a separate step, applies the minimum set of DOM changes. The react.dev guide "Render and Commit" uses a restaurant analogy: the trigger is a customer placing an order, the render is the kitchen preparing the dish, and the commit is the waiter putting the plate on the table. Keeping these three phases apart in your head is the single most useful thing for reasoning about React performance and bugs. ## The three phases ```text trigger render (pure, can be thrown away) commit (side effects, never interrupted) ------- --------------------------------- ---------------------------------------- setState() --> call components top-down from the --> apply DOM mutations initial root component that changed update refs context change build the new element tree run useLayoutEffect (sync, before paint) parent re-render diff against the current fiber tree browser paints mark fibers with effect flags run useEffect (after paint, usually) ``` **Trigger.** Only two things start a render: the initial `root.render()` call, and a state update (`setState`, a `useReducer` dispatch, a context value change, or an external store notifying `useSyncExternalStore`). Props changing is not a trigger by itself; props change *because* a parent re-rendered. **Render.** React calls the component that scheduled the update, then recursively every component it returns, unless it can bail out. Rendering must be **pure**: same props, state and context in, same JSX out, no mutations of anything that existed before the render. React relies on this purity in three ways: it may render a component twice in development (Strict Mode) to surface impurity, it may start a render and throw it away (concurrent rendering), and the React Compiler assumes it when it memoises. **Commit.** React walks the list of fibers flagged with changes and performs the DOM operations: insert, update attributes and text, remove. This phase is synchronous and cannot be interrupted, because a half-applied DOM would be visible to the user. After mutations React attaches refs, runs layout effects synchronously (so you can measure the DOM before the browser paints), yields to the browser to paint, and then runs passive effects (`useEffect`). A consequence people get wrong in interviews: **a component that re-renders but produces identical output causes no DOM work.** The cost of an unnecessary re-render is the JavaScript time to call the function and diff its output, not a repaint. That is cheap for small components and expensive for a 5,000-row table. ## Why a component re-renders Josh Comeau's "Why React Re-Renders" states the rule cleanly: **every re-render in React starts with a state change, and when a component re-renders, all of its descendants re-render too** (unless something stops it). People often believe "a component re-renders when its props change". That is backwards. A child re-renders because its parent rendered; whether the props changed is irrelevant unless the child is wrapped in `memo`. | Cause | Example | Does the child re-render? | |---|---|---| | Own state update | `setOpen(true)` inside `Menu` | `Menu` and its whole subtree | | Parent re-render | `App` updates `count`; `Sidebar` gets no props | Yes, `Sidebar` re-renders anyway | | Context change | Provider value changes | Every consumer of that context, even through `memo` | | `memo` child, same props | `memo(Row)` with stable props | No, React bails out | | `memo` child, new object prop | `` | Yes, a new object every render breaks the shallow compare | React also has a cheap built-in bailout: if you call `setState` with a value that is `Object.is` equal to the current state, React skips re-rendering children (it may still call the component itself once before bailing). ## Reconciliation: how the diff works Comparing two arbitrary trees optimally is roughly O(n^3). React makes it O(n) with two heuristics, documented since the original reconciliation docs: 1. **Elements of different types produce different trees.** If a `div` becomes a `section`, or `` becomes ``, React unmounts the old subtree (destroying its state and DOM) and mounts a new one. It does not try to reuse anything below. 2. **Keys identify children across renders.** Within a list of siblings, React matches old and new children by `key`. Without keys, it matches by index. The comparison happens on **fibers**. A fiber is React's internal unit of work: one per component instance or host element, holding its type, key, props, state (the hook list), and pointers to its parent, first child and next sibling. React keeps two trees: the **current** tree (what is on screen) and the **work-in-progress** tree (being rendered). When a render finishes, the work-in-progress tree becomes current in a single pointer swap during commit. That double buffering is what lets React abandon a render halfway without corrupting what the user sees. ### State lives at a position in the tree The react.dev page "Preserving and Resetting State" makes a point that trips up even experienced developers: **state is tied to a position in the render tree, not to the component or the JSX expression.** React preserves a component's state as long as the same component type renders at the same position. ```text {isFancy ? : } -> same type, same position: state is PRESERVED when isFancy flips {isPaused ?

Paused

: } -> different type at that position: Counter is UNMOUNTED, state lost -> new key: React treats it as a different component, state RESET ``` Defining a component inside another component is the classic bug that follows from this. A nested `function Input() {}` is a new function object on every render, so its type changes every render, so React unmounts and remounts it, and the input loses focus after each keystroke. ## Keys, properly A key tells React "this child is the same item as last time, even if it moved". With keys React can move existing DOM nodes and keep component state attached to the right item. What goes wrong with `key={index}`: - **Reordering, inserting at the top or filtering** shifts indexes, so state (an uncontrolled input's text, an expanded flag, focus) stays at the index and ends up attached to a different item. - **Performance**: inserting at the start makes every row look "changed", so React updates every row instead of inserting one node. Index keys are fine only when the list is static: never reordered, filtered or inserted into, and items have no state. Keys must be stable, unique among siblings (not globally), and not generated during render (`key={Math.random()}` remounts every row every render, which is worse than no key). Keys also work outside lists. `` is the idiomatic way to **reset** all state inside a form when the selected user changes, instead of syncing state in an effect. ## Batching React groups multiple state updates into one render. Since **React 18, batching is automatic everywhere**: inside event handlers, promises, `setTimeout`, native event listeners and anything else, as long as you use `createRoot`. Before 18 it only batched inside React event handlers, so two `setState` calls in a `fetch().then()` caused two renders. ```text onClick: setCount(c => c + 1); setFlag(f => !f); setText('hi') -> one render, one commit (React 18+) ``` Two details that come up: - State updates are **queued**, not applied immediately. Reading `count` right after `setCount(count + 1)` gives the old value, because `count` is a constant captured by this render's closure. Use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the next value depends on the previous one, especially when calling it multiple times. - `flushSync(() => setX(...))` from `react-dom` forces a synchronous render and commit, for the rare case where you must read the updated DOM immediately (scrolling to a newly added item). It is a performance escape hatch, not a habit.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

React rendering questions separate people who have used React from people who can debug it. The interviewer wants to hear that you know rendering is calling functions, not touching the DOM; that re-renders cascade from state changes down the tree; that identity (type, position, key) decides whether state survives; and that memoisation is a targeted tool you apply after measuring, now mostly automated by the compiler. Senior candidates are expected to connect this to user-facing metrics: unnecessary renders become long tasks, which become poor INP.

## Question 1: "What happens when you call setState?"

**Model answer (about 60 seconds):**

> setState does not change the variable in the current render. It queues an update on that component's fiber and asks the scheduler for a render at a priority based on where the update came from: a click is high priority, a transition is lower. React batches all updates queued in the same tick into one render. In the render phase React calls the component with the new state and then its children, building a work-in-progress tree and diffing it against the current one. Children wrapped in memo with equal props are skipped. Then the commit phase applies the DOM changes in one go, runs layout effects before paint, and passive effects after paint. If the new state is Object.is equal to the old one, React bails out early.

Follow-ups: "Why does logging state right after setState show the old value?" (each render's state is a constant captured by closures; the new value exists in the next render). "When would you use the updater form?" (when the next state depends on the previous, or several updates are queued).

## Question 2: "Why is `key={index}` a problem?"

**Model answer:** Keys tell React which child is which across renders. With index keys, identity follows position, so when you insert at the top, filter or sort, React thinks the item at index 0 is the same component as before and keeps its state and DOM. An uncontrolled input's text or an expanded flag then appears on the wrong item, and React also updates every row instead of moving or inserting one. Index keys are acceptable only for static lists with no item state. Use a stable id from the data; never generate keys during render.

Bonus point: keys are also a tool to reset state on purpose, such as `<Form key={userId} />`.

## Question 3: "Explain reconciliation."

**Model answer:** A general tree diff is cubic, so React uses two heuristics to make it linear. Different element types at the same position mean a different subtree, so React unmounts and remounts rather than trying to reuse. Among siblings, keys match children across renders. The work happens on fibers: React keeps the current tree and builds a work-in-progress tree, and swaps them at commit. Because rendering is separate from committing and the work-in-progress tree is private, React can pause, resume or discard a render without the user seeing an inconsistent UI, which is the foundation of concurrent features.

## Question 4: "When do you use memo, useMemo and useCallback? Do you still need them with the React Compiler?"

**Model answer:**

> They are about skipping work across renders, not making code faster. memo skips re-rendering a component when its props are shallowly equal; useMemo caches an expensive computed value; useCallback keeps a function's identity stable so a memoised child or an effect does not see a new function. They only work in combination, and one inline object breaks the chain. Before reaching for them I restructure: move state down, pass expensive subtrees as children, split contexts. With the React Compiler, the build inserts this memoisation automatically and more granularly, so new code rarely needs the manual hooks. The compiler needs code that follows the Rules of React, so the ESLint rules matter. And it does not fix necessary work: huge lists still need virtualisation, and a single context holding everything still re-renders all consumers.

## Question 5: "A component re-renders on every keystroke elsewhere on the page. How do you find out why?"

**Model answer:**

1. Turn on "Highlight updates when components render" in React DevTools and reproduce.
2. Record in the Profiler with "Record why each component rendered" enabled.
3. Typical causes: the state lives too high (move it down), the component consumes a context that changes on each keystroke (split the context or use a selector store), or a parent passes a new object, array or function each render to a memoised child.
4. Fix structurally first, then memoise. Verify with the Profiler and, if this was an INP problem, with a Performance panel recording.

## Question 6: "Why does my input lose focus after every keystroke?"

**Model answer:** Almost always a component defined inside another component, or a key that changes every render. A nested component function is a new type on each render, so React unmounts the old input and mounts a new one. Move the component definition to module scope, and make sure keys are stable.

## Code question: predict the output

```tsx
function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  function onClick() {
    setN(n + 1);
    setN(n + 1);
    setN((x) => x + 1);
    console.log(n);
  }
  return <button onClick={onClick}>{n}</button>;
}
```

**Answer:** The log prints `0`, because `n` is the value from this render. After the batched render the button shows `2`: the first two updates both compute `0 + 1`, and the updater then turns `1` into `2`. Explaining *why* (closures over the render's state, a queue of updates processed in order) scores more than the number.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Does a re-render always update the DOM?" | No. Render produces a description; commit changes only what differs |
| "What does Strict Mode double-invoke and why?" | Component bodies, initialisers and effects (mount, unmount, mount) in development, to expose impure renders and missing cleanups |
| "useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?" | Layout effects run synchronously after DOM mutation and before paint (measure, then adjust without flicker); passive effects run after paint |
| "What is flushSync?" | Forces a synchronous render and commit; for reading updated DOM immediately; costs responsiveness |
| "Does context bypass memo?" | Yes, a consumer re-renders when the context value changes even if its parent bailed out |
| "Is the virtual DOM what makes React fast?" | It makes updates declarative and predictable; speed comes from doing less work, which is your job and the compiler's |

## Common mistakes

- Saying components re-render "when props change". They re-render when an ancestor or themselves render, or a consumed context changes.
- Wrapping everything in `useMemo`/`useCallback` without a memoised consumer, which adds cost for nothing.
- Using effects to derive state, causing an extra render per change.
- Mutating state objects in place (`items.push(x); setItems(items)`): same reference, so React bails out and the UI does not update.
- Treating the React Compiler as a fix for slow commits or huge DOMs.
- Forgetting that state is tied to position and type, then being surprised when it survives (same type) or resets (type changed).

complexity.time: JS cost only, no DOM work

keyPoints: Rendering means calling components to describe UI; the commit phase applies the minimal DOM changes and cannot be interrupted.
Every re-render starts with a state change, and a rendering component re-renders all descendants unless memo or a structural pattern stops it.
Reconciliation is linear because different types replace subtrees and keys match siblings; state is tied to type and position in the tree.
Index keys attach state to positions, so reordering or inserting moves state to the wrong item; a changed key resets state on purpose.
React 18+ batches all updates in the same tick into one render, everywhere; setState values are snapshots of the current render.
Restructure first (move state down, children as props, split contexts), then memoise; manual memo, useMemo and useCallback only work together.
The React Compiler 1.0 auto-memoises code that follows the Rules of React, but does not fix necessary work like huge lists or context churn.

check.q: A parent re-renders because its own state changed. Its child is not wrapped in memo and receives no props. What happens to the child?
options: It does not re-render because its props did not change
It re-renders, but React commits no DOM changes if its output is identical
It is unmounted and remounted
It re-renders only in development Strict Mode
check.why: Without memo, children re-render whenever their parent renders, regardless of props. Rendering only calls the function and diffs; if the output is the same, the commit touches nothing.

check.q: A list uses key={index}. The user types into the first row's input, then a new item is inserted at the top. What does the user see?
options: The typed text stays with the item it was typed into
All inputs are cleared
The typed text now appears in the new first row, attached to the wrong item
React throws a duplicate key error
check.why: With index keys, identity follows position. The component at index 0 keeps its state and DOM, so the draft text now sits next to the newly inserted item.

check.q: Which problem does the React Compiler NOT solve on its own?
options: Children re-rendering because a parent passes a new inline object each render
Forgetting useCallback for a handler passed to a memoised child
Recomputing an expensive derived value on every render
Committing 10,000 DOM rows when a large list genuinely changes
check.why: The compiler removes unnecessary renders by caching values and JSX. Rendering and committing a huge list that really changed is necessary work; virtualisation or transitions address it.

lessons.title: React Server Components and Server Actions
lessons.summary: What Server Components are (and are not), the use client boundary, what can be serialised across it, the RSC payload, streaming with Suspense, Server Actions as public endpoints, and caching.

parts.label: Boundaries and payload
parts.body:
## The idea in plain words

For most of React's life, every component you wrote ran in the browser. Even with server-side rendering (SSR), the server only produced a first HTML snapshot; then the browser downloaded the code for every component and re-ran it during hydration. **React Server Components (RSC)** split components into two kinds that live in one tree:

- **Server Components** run only on the server, at build time or per request. Their code, and every library they import, is never sent to the browser. They can be `async` and read databases, files or internal services directly.
- **Client Components** are the ones you already know: they can use state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs. They are rendered to HTML on the server for the first paint (yes, Client Components are also SSR'd) and then hydrate in the browser.

Dan Abramov's essay "The Two Reacts" frames it as one program that spans two computers: some of your UI wants to run close to the data (the server), some close to the user (the browser), and RSC lets one component tree express both. A good analogy is a restaurant: the kitchen (server) prepares dishes with ingredients the customer never sees, and only the plate plus a few interactive pieces (salt shaker, a menu you can flip) reach the table.

## Server Components are not SSR

This is the most common confusion, and interviewers probe it directly.

| | SSR (classic) | Server Components |
|---|---|---|
| Output | HTML string or stream | RSC payload: a serialised React tree (and HTML on first load via SSR) |
| Runs again in the browser? | Yes, every component hydrates | No, server components never run in the browser |
| Code shipped | All components | Only client components |
| On client navigation | Usually fetch JSON and render on client | Fetch a new RSC payload and merge it into the tree, keeping client state |
| Can refetch a subtree from the server? | No | Yes (router refresh, server actions revalidation) |

In frameworks like Next.js App Router, both happen: Server Components produce the RSC payload, and SSR turns the combined tree (server output plus client components) into HTML for the first paint. Then only client components hydrate.

## The boundary: `"use client"`

By default, in an RSC framework, every component is a Server Component. The `"use client"` directive at the top of a file marks a **boundary**: that module and everything it imports become part of the client bundle.

```text
app/page.tsx          (server)   imports ProductInfo, AddToCart
  ProductInfo.tsx     (server)   reads DB, renders markdown with a 60 KB library -> 0 KB shipped
  AddToCart.tsx       "use client" -> shipped, hydrates
    QuantityPicker.tsx (no directive, but imported by a client module) -> also client
```

Rules that follow from this:

1. **The directive marks a module boundary, not a component.** Everything a client module imports is client code. You do not need `"use client"` in every interactive file, only at the entry points from the server side.
2. **A Server Component can render a Client Component and pass it props.** The props must be serialisable (next section).
3. **A Client Component cannot import a Server Component**, because importing makes it client code. But a Client Component can **receive** Server Component output as `children` or any JSX prop. The server renders that subtree and slots the result in. This "donut" pattern keeps big server-rendered content inside an interactive wrapper (a tab panel, a modal, a collapsible).
4. **Push the boundary down.** Marking a layout or page `"use client"` turns the whole subtree into client code and throws away the benefit. Keep the client part to the leaf that needs interactivity: the button, not the card.

There is also the `server-only` package: importing it from a module makes the build fail if that module is ever pulled into client code, which protects secrets and database clients from leaking by accident. Its counterpart `client-only` guards browser-only modules.

## Serialisation: what can cross the boundary

When a Server Component renders a Client Component, React must send the props over the network, so they must be serialisable by React's RSC protocol (often called Flight). The react.dev reference for `"use client"` lists what is allowed:

| Allowed | Not allowed |
|---|---|
| Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, globally registered symbols (`Symbol.for`) | Ordinary functions and event handlers (except Server Functions) |
| Arrays, Map, Set, typed arrays, ArrayBuffer, iterables of serialisable values | Class instances (your own `User` class, a Mongoose document) |
| `Date` | Objects with a null prototype |
| Plain objects of serialisable values | Non-registered symbols |
| JSX elements (server or client) | Things that only make sense in one process: DB connections, sockets |
| Promises (the client can read them with `use`) | |
| Server Functions (marked `"use server"`) | |

Practical consequences:

- **You cannot pass `onClick` from a Server Component.** Event handlers live in Client Components. If the server needs to provide behaviour, pass a Server Function (an action), which travels as a reference id, not as code.
- **Database documents must be mapped to plain objects.** Passing an ORM model instance fails or leaks fields. Map to a DTO with only the fields the client needs. Everything you pass is visible in the page's payload, so never pass a whole user record with a password hash or internal flags.
- **Promises can be passed down.** A Server Component can start a fetch, pass the unresolved promise to a Client Component, and the client unwraps it with `use(promise)` inside a Suspense boundary. The data streams in when it resolves.

## What the RSC payload looks like

You rarely read it, but knowing its shape explains a lot of behaviour. It is a line-oriented stream of chunks. Each chunk has an id; later chunks can fill in "holes" referenced by earlier ones:

```text
1:I["./add-to-cart.tsx",["chunk-a1b2.js"],"AddToCart"]      <- client module reference
0:["$","main",null,{"children":[
     ["$","h1",null,{"children":"Trail shoe"}],
     ["$","$L1",null,{"sku":"42","price":129}],            <- render client component 1 with props
     ["$","$Sreact.suspense",null,{"fallback":"...","children":"$L2"}]
   ]}]
2:["$","ul",null,{"children":[ ...reviews... ]}]            <- streamed later, fills hole $L2
```

The browser's React runtime reads this, loads the referenced client chunks, and reconciles the tree. On a client-side navigation, the router asks the server for the payload of the new route segment only, and React merges it in. Client component state in shared layouts survives because those fibers keep their type and position.

## What you gain and what you pay

**Gains:**

- **Less JavaScript.** Markdown renderers, syntax highlighters, date and i18n libraries, and data-access code stay on the server. Only interactive leaves ship.
- **No client-server waterfalls for data.** A Server Component awaits its data next to the database, so the browser does not do "download bundle, then fetch, then render".
- **Secrets stay server-side,** and access control can happen where the data is read.
- **Composable data fetching.** Each component fetches what it needs; with request memoisation (`React.cache`) duplicate reads in one request are deduplicated.

**Costs:**

- A new mental model: two module graphs, serialisation rules, and "where does this code run?" for every file.
- Framework coupling: RSC needs a bundler and router integration (Next.js App Router is the most mature; React Router and others have added support).
- Server work per request, so caching becomes a central design concern.
- Debugging spans two environments; errors in Server Components show up in server logs and the error overlay, not in the browser console.
- A new attack surface: the RSC protocol and Server Functions are network-facing deserialisation endpoints. In December 2025 the React team disclosed CVE-2025-55182, a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the RSC payload handling of the `react-server-dom-*` packages, fixed in 19.0.1, 19.1.2 and 19.2.1, with further advisories after that. The lesson: treat RSC framework and React patch releases as security updates and apply them quickly.

parts.label: Streaming and actions
parts.body:
## Streaming: sending the tree as it becomes ready

A Server Component tree often depends on several data sources with very different latencies: the product row is in a cache (5 ms), reviews come from a slow service (400 ms), recommendations from an ML endpoint (900 ms). Without streaming, the response waits for the slowest one. With streaming, React sends what is ready and leaves **holes** wrapped in `<Suspense>` boundaries, then fills them as data arrives, all in one HTTP response.

Step by step for a first page load in an RSC framework:

```text
t=0     request arrives; React starts rendering the server tree
t=10ms  product data ready; ProductInfo renders; Reviews and Recs suspend
t=15ms  flush: HTML for shell + product + fallbacks, plus the first RSC chunks
        browser paints, starts fetching CSS and client chunks
t=60ms  client chunks loaded; React hydrates the shell and AddToCart (selective hydration)
t=400ms reviews resolve -> server streams an HTML fragment + RSC chunk; React swaps the fallback
t=900ms recs resolve -> same
```

Details that matter:

- **Where you put `Suspense` decides what streams.** An `await` at the top of the page blocks everything below it. Move slow awaits into child components wrapped in `Suspense`, or start the fetch early and pass the promise down.
- **Fallbacks should be the same size as the content** to avoid layout shift (CLS).
- **Status code and headers are sent with the first flush.** A `notFound()` or redirect triggered after streaming has started cannot change the HTTP status; frameworks handle that by rendering an error UI or injecting a client redirect. Decide 404s before the first flush where it matters for SEO.
- **Buffering breaks streaming.** Some proxies, compression setups or serverless adapters buffer the whole response. Check that chunks actually arrive incrementally (`curl -N` shows it).
- **Parallel, not sequential.** Two independent `await`s in a row form a waterfall. Use `Promise.all`, or split them into sibling components under separate boundaries so each streams independently.

On client-side navigations the same mechanism applies to the RSC payload: the router shows the nearest `loading.tsx` or Suspense fallback immediately and streams the new segment in.

## Server Functions and Server Actions

A **Server Function** is an async function marked with `"use server"` (either inline in a Server Component or in a module whose top says `"use server"`). It runs on the server, but Client Components can call it like a normal async function. The react.dev docs call these Server Functions; when used for mutations through a form `action` or inside a transition they are called **Server Actions**, which is also Next.js's name.

How a call actually works:

```text
Client: <form action={addToCart}> submit, or await addToCart(sku) from a handler
  -> framework sends POST to the current URL with an action id header and serialised arguments
Server: looks up the function by id, deserialises arguments, runs it
  -> may mutate data, revalidate caches, redirect
  -> responds with the return value AND, if caches were revalidated, the updated RSC payload
Client: React applies the new payload in the same round trip (no separate refetch)
```

What makes them pleasant:

- **Progressive enhancement.** `<form action={serverAction}>` works before JavaScript has loaded; the framework turns it into a normal POST, and once hydrated React intercepts it.
- **One round trip for mutate plus refresh.** After `revalidatePath('/cart')` or a tag invalidation, the response carries the fresh server tree.
- **Integrated pending and optimistic states** through React 19 hooks: `useActionState` (result and pending flag of an action), `useFormStatus` (pending state of the parent form, for a submit button), and `useOptimistic` (show the expected result immediately, roll back if the action fails).

### Server Functions are public endpoints

This is the point that separates seniors. A Server Function is reachable by anyone who can send a POST to your app with the right action id; the id is in your client bundle. So inside **every** Server Function:

1. **Authenticate and authorise.** Call your session check and verify the user may touch this resource. Do not rely on the button being hidden.
2. **Validate arguments with a schema** (zod or similar). The TypeScript signature is not enforced at runtime; arguments arrive from the network.
3. **Return minimal data.** Whatever you return is serialised to the client.
4. **Treat closures carefully.** Inline server functions that close over variables from a Server Component send those values to the client and back (Next.js encrypts them, but encryption is not authorisation). Prefer passing ids and re-reading on the server.

Next.js adds some defences: action ids are not guessable from function names, unused actions are not exposed, and POSTs whose `Origin` does not match the host are rejected by default (a CSRF defence), configurable with `serverActions.allowedOrigins`. These are guard rails, not a substitute for steps 1 and 2.

## Caching and data in an RSC app

With components fetching their own data on the server, "how often does this run?" is the central question. The layers, from short-lived to long-lived:

| Layer | Scope | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Request memoisation | One render pass | `React.cache(fn)` dedupes identical calls in a request |
| Component or function cache | Across requests | Next.js 16 Cache Components: `'use cache'` with `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` |
| Route output | Static prerender or partial prerender | Static shell served from the CDN, dynamic holes streamed |
| Client router cache | One browser session | Prefetched and visited segments reused on navigation |

Invalidation is event-driven: after a mutation, call `updateTag(tag)` inside a Server Action when the user must immediately see their own write, `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for stale-while-revalidate behaviour, or `revalidatePath(path)`. Getting this wrong produces the two classic RSC bugs: "I saved but the page shows old data" (forgot to invalidate) and "user A sees user B's data" (cached something personalised in a shared cache). Personalised data must be read from cookies or headers inside dynamic, uncached code, never inside a shared cached function.

## Patterns that work

- **Fetch in the Server Component that needs the data,** and use `React.cache` so the same query called from a layout and a page runs once.
- **Start promises early, await late.** Kick off fetches at the top, pass promises down, and let `Suspense` boundaries decide what blocks.
- **Keep client components as leaves** that receive plain props, and use the children pattern for interactive wrappers around server content.
- **Use a data-access layer** (a module imported only from the server, guarded with `server-only`) that performs authorisation checks and returns DTOs. Components call it instead of talking to the database directly.
- **Third-party components without `"use client"`** that use hooks will fail when imported from a Server Component. Wrap them in your own small client module that re-exports them.

## Failure modes and debugging

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components" | Passing an event handler or callback from server to client | Move the handler into the client component, or pass a Server Function |
| "useState only works in Client Components" | Hook used in a server module | Add `"use client"` to the leaf that needs it |
| Bundle suddenly much bigger | `"use client"` added high in the tree, or a client module imports a heavy library | Push the boundary down; check the bundle analyser |
| Secret appears in browser payload | Passed a whole object as a prop | Map to a DTO; add `server-only` to data modules; consider taint APIs |
| Page waits for slowest query | Top-level sequential `await`s | `Promise.all`, or move slow parts behind `Suspense` |
| Stale data after mutation | Missing invalidation | `updateTag`, `revalidateTag`, `revalidatePath` in the action |
| Hydration mismatch in a client component | Time, randomness or `window` checks during render | Render that content after mount, or pass the server value as a prop |

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

RSC questions check whether you understand **where code runs and what crosses the network**. Weak answers say "Server Components are SSR" or "they make everything faster". Strong answers explain the two module graphs, the serialisation boundary, what the payload contains, how streaming and Suspense interact, and the security posture of Server Actions. For senior roles, expect a design question: "how would you structure this page with server and client components?"

## Question 1: "What is the difference between Server Components and SSR?"

**Model answer:**

> SSR is a rendering technique: run components on the server to produce HTML for the first paint, then download all their code and hydrate in the browser. Server Components are a component type: they run only on the server, their code never ships, and they produce a serialised React tree, the RSC payload, rather than HTML. In practice frameworks use both: Server Components produce the payload, SSR turns the combined tree into HTML for the first load, and then only Client Components hydrate. On client navigation the router fetches a new RSC payload and merges it in without losing client state, which plain SSR cannot do.

## Question 2: "Can a Client Component render a Server Component?"

**Model answer:** It cannot import one, because anything imported by a `"use client"` module becomes client code. But it can render Server Component output passed to it as `children` or another JSX prop. The parent Server Component renders both, and the client component just places the already-rendered subtree. This is how you build an interactive tab strip or modal around server-rendered content without shipping that content's code.

## Question 3: "What can you pass as props from a Server Component to a Client Component?"

**Model answer:** Values React can serialise: primitives, plain objects and arrays, Map, Set, Date, typed arrays, JSX, promises and Server Functions. Not regular functions, class instances, or anything tied to the server process. In practice I map database rows to small DTOs, because every prop ends up in the page payload, visible to the user. Event handlers stay in client components; if the server needs to provide behaviour, I pass a Server Action.

## Question 4: "How do Server Actions work, and what are the security implications?"

**Model answer:**

> A Server Action is an async function marked `"use server"`. The client gets a reference id; calling it, or submitting a form whose action is that function, sends a POST with the id and serialised arguments. The server runs it, and if it revalidated cached data the response includes the updated server tree, so mutation and refresh are one round trip. Forms work before hydration. Security-wise, each action is a public HTTP endpoint: anyone can call it with arbitrary arguments. So every action authenticates, authorises against the resource, validates input with a schema, and returns only what the client needs. Frameworks add Origin checks against CSRF and unguessable ids, but those do not replace auth checks. The RSC protocol itself is attack surface too, as the critical December 2025 React advisory showed, so we patch React and the framework promptly.

## Question 5: "Design the server/client split for a dashboard with a sidebar, a filterable table and a chart."

**Model answer, structured:**

1. **Layout and sidebar:** Server Components. The nav items come from the user's permissions, read on the server. The active-link highlight is a tiny client component using the pathname.
2. **Filters:** a client component that writes filters to the URL search params, so the state is shareable and the server can read it.
3. **Table data:** a Server Component that reads `searchParams`, queries through a data-access layer that enforces tenant access, and renders rows. Sorting and pagination also live in the URL. If rows need inline editing, each editable cell is a client component calling a Server Action.
4. **Chart:** the charting library is heavy and needs the DOM, so the chart is a client component loaded lazily, receiving pre-aggregated data computed on the server.
5. **Streaming:** the table and chart each sit in their own `Suspense` boundary with same-size skeletons, so a slow aggregation does not block the table.
6. **Caching:** reference data (product catalogue) cached with tags; per-user data dynamic. Mutations call `updateTag` for the affected tag.

## Question 6: "Your page got slower after migrating to the App Router. What do you check?"

**Model answer:** First, sequential awaits at the top of pages and layouts creating a server-side waterfall: parallelise or move slow parts behind Suspense. Second, `"use client"` placed too high, which brings large subtrees and libraries back into the bundle: check the bundle analyser and push boundaries down. Third, missing caching, so every request hits slow services: add tagged caching for shared data. Fourth, streaming being buffered by the hosting setup, so TTFB equals the slowest query. Measure TTFB, LCP and INP before and after to know which one regressed.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Can Server Components use hooks?" | No `useState`, `useEffect` or context. They are `async` and `await` data directly, and can use helpers like `React.cache` |
| "Are Client Components rendered on the server?" | Yes, for the initial HTML; they also hydrate and run in the browser |
| "What does `server-only` do?" | Makes the build fail if a module is imported into client code; protects secrets and DB clients |
| "Why pass a promise to a client component?" | Start the fetch on the server without blocking; the client reads it with `use` inside Suspense, and data streams in |
| "How do you show a pending state for an action?" | `useActionState` or `useFormStatus` for pending, `useOptimistic` for instant feedback with rollback |
| "What happens to client state on navigation?" | Shared layout fibers keep type and position, so their state is preserved; only the changed segment updates |

## Common mistakes

- Calling Server Components "SSR" or claiming they replace client state management. Interactivity still lives in client components.
- Adding `"use client"` to a layout or page to fix one hook error, shipping the whole subtree.
- Passing ORM objects or full user records as props, leaking fields into the payload.
- Skipping auth and validation in Server Actions because "only our button calls it".
- Awaiting everything at the top of the page and then wondering why streaming does not help.
- Caching personalised data in a shared cache.

keyPoints: Server Components run only on the server and never ship their code; Client Components are SSR'd for first paint and then hydrate.
use client marks a module boundary: everything a client module imports becomes client code, so push the boundary down to interactive leaves.
Client Components cannot import Server Components but can render server output passed as children (the donut pattern).
Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable: primitives, plain objects, Map, Set, Date, JSX, promises and Server Functions, not handlers or class instances.
Streaming sends ready parts first and fills Suspense holes later in one response; top-level sequential awaits defeat it.
Server Actions are public POST endpoints: authenticate, authorise, validate with a schema and return minimal data in every one.
Caching decides cost: React.cache per request, tagged caches across requests, and event-driven invalidation after mutations.

check.q: A Server Component renders <Chart onPointClick={(p) => log(p)} />, where Chart is a Client Component. What happens?
options: It works; the function is serialised and sent to the browser
It fails: plain functions cannot be serialised across the server-client boundary
It works only if Chart is wrapped in memo
The function runs on the server whenever a point is clicked
check.why: Only serialisable values cross the boundary. Regular functions cannot; the handler must live inside a Client Component, or the server can pass a Server Function marked use server.

check.q: Which statement about Server Actions is correct?
options: They are private because only components in your app can call them
TypeScript types on their parameters are enforced at runtime
They are reachable by direct POST requests, so each must check auth and validate input
They cannot return data to the client
check.why: The action id ships in the client bundle and the call is an HTTP POST, so anyone can invoke it with arbitrary arguments. Auth, authorisation and schema validation belong inside every action.

check.q: A page awaits a 900 ms recommendations query at the top before returning JSX. What is the best fix to improve first paint?
options: Move the query into a child Server Component wrapped in Suspense with a same-size fallback
Mark the page use client and fetch in useEffect
Wrap the page in memo
Add a longer HTTP cache on the HTML for every user
check.why: The top-level await blocks the whole response. Behind a Suspense boundary the shell streams immediately and the slow part fills in later; moving to the client adds a waterfall and more JS.

parts.label: Suspense
parts.body:
## What "concurrent" means in React

Before React 18, rendering was one uninterruptible chunk of work: once React started rendering an update, it finished, however long it took. Typing into a search box that re-rendered a 3,000-item list froze the input for the whole render. **Concurrent rendering** changes one thing: React can **prepare a new UI in the background, pause to handle something more urgent, and throw away work that became obsolete**, while the screen keeps showing a consistent version of the UI.

An analogy: a chef (the main thread) preparing a big banquet order (a heavy re-render). A waiter brings a quick order for a single coffee (a keystroke). A non-concurrent chef finishes the whole banquet first. A concurrent chef pauses, makes the coffee, then resumes the banquet, and if the banquet order changes halfway, throws away the half-made dish instead of serving it.

Concurrency is not parallelism. It still runs on one main thread. It works because the render phase is pure and builds a private work-in-progress tree (see the rendering-model lesson); nothing reaches the screen until commit, so abandoning a render is safe.

You opt into concurrency per update, through three features:

| Feature | What it tells React |
|---|---|
| `<Suspense>` | "This part of the tree may not be ready; show this fallback meanwhile" |
| `startTransition` / `useTransition` | "This update is not urgent; keep the current UI responsive and interruptible" |
| `useDeferredValue` | "Render with the old value first, then catch up with the new one in the background" |

## Suspense: declarative loading states

`<Suspense fallback={...}>` wraps a part of the tree. When any component inside it **suspends**, meaning it cannot render yet because something it needs is still loading, React shows the nearest boundary's fallback instead of that whole subtree. When the data is ready, React retries rendering and replaces the fallback.

What can suspend:

1. **Lazy-loaded code:** `const Chart = lazy(() => import('./chart'))`.
2. **Reading a promise with `use(promise)`** (React 19), where the promise is cached or created on the server and passed down. A promise created fresh during a client render would restart every render, so it must come from a cache, a framework or a Server Component.
3. **Suspense-enabled data frameworks:** Next.js Server Components with `async` components, Relay, TanStack Query's `useSuspenseQuery`, SWR's suspense mode.

Fetching in `useEffect` does **not** trigger Suspense; the component already rendered with no data.

### Step by step on a small example

```tsx
<Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
  <Header />
  <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
    <Feed />            {/* suspends: waiting for posts */}
  </Suspense>
  <Sidebar />           {/* suspends: waiting for profile */}
</Suspense>
```

- `Feed` suspends: the inner boundary shows `FeedSkeleton`, and the rest can still appear.
- `Sidebar` suspends: it has no boundary of its own, so the **outer** boundary shows `PageSkeleton` until the sidebar is ready. Then the header and sidebar appear, and the feed area still shows its skeleton until the posts arrive.

Boundary placement is a design decision: **each boundary is a unit that appears together.** Put boundaries around things that make sense to load independently, matching how a designer would want the page to reveal, not around every component (which produces a "popcorn" UI of spinners). React also throttles reveals slightly, so several boundaries finishing close together appear in one go.

### Suspense behaviour you should know

- **Already-visible content is not replaced by a fallback during a transition.** If an update suspends content that is already on screen, React would normally show the fallback again (jarring: a page flashes to a skeleton). If the update is wrapped in `startTransition`, React instead keeps showing the old UI until the new one is ready. Routers wrap navigations in transitions for exactly this reason.
- **React 19 commits fallbacks sooner.** When a component suspends, React 19 shows the nearest fallback immediately and then "pre-warms" (renders in the background) the suspended siblings, instead of first rendering all siblings before showing any fallback.
- **State inside a boundary that shows its fallback for the first time is not kept**, because those components never mounted. Once mounted, hiding behind a fallback later preserves their state.
- **Errors are separate.** Suspense handles "not ready yet"; an error boundary handles "failed". Wrap data regions in both, and give the error boundary a retry.
- **Use `key` to reset a boundary**, for example `<Suspense key={query}>` so a new search shows the fallback instead of keeping stale results.

## Suspense on the server

The same boundaries drive **streaming SSR**. React sends HTML for everything outside suspended boundaries plus the fallbacks, then streams the content of each boundary as its data resolves (the reactwg discussion "New Suspense SSR Architecture in React 18" is still the clearest explanation). Each boundary also **hydrates independently** (selective hydration): React can hydrate the header before the feed's code has loaded, and if the user clicks inside a not-yet-hydrated boundary, React prioritises hydrating that one. Suspense is therefore the single tool for both "show a skeleton while loading" and "do not let the slowest part of the page block everything".

## Activity: hidden but alive

React 19.2 added `<Activity mode="visible" | "hidden">`. Hidden content is visually hidden, its effects are cleaned up, and its updates are rendered at the lowest priority, but its **state is preserved**, and React can pre-render it in the background. Use cases: keeping the state of an inactive tab, or pre-rendering the next screen a user is likely to open. It replaces the old choice between unmounting (losing state) and hiding with CSS (keeping effects and updates running at full cost).

  Suspended --> OldUIKept: update inside a transition and content already visible
  FallbackShown --> Retrying: promise resolves
  OldUIKept --> Retrying: promise resolves

  Retrying --> Suspended: something else suspends

parts.label: Transitions and lanes
parts.body:
## Urgent vs non-urgent updates Not all state updates are equally important to the user. Typing a character, clicking a button, or pressing a key should feel instant: users expect the input to reflect their action within one frame. Updating the filtered list below the input, switching the content of a tab, or navigating to a new page can take a little longer, as long as the UI stays responsive meanwhile. React lets you mark the second kind as a **transition**: ```tsx const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); function onChange(e: React.ChangeEvent) { setText(e.target.value); // urgent: the input must update now startTransition(() => { setQuery(e.target.value); // non-urgent: re-render the big list }); } ``` What React does with a transition update: 1. It renders the transition **in the background** with interruptible time slicing. Every few milliseconds the work loop checks whether something more urgent is waiting and yields to the browser. 2. If a new urgent update arrives (the next keystroke), React handles it first, then restarts the transition with the latest state. Intermediate transition renders that became stale are **discarded**, never committed. 3. While the transition is in progress, `isPending` is `true`, so you can dim the old results or show a subtle spinner, instead of replacing content with a fallback. 4. If the transition suspends on data, React keeps showing the current UI (it does not flash a fallback for already-visible content) until the new UI is ready. Rules and caveats from the react.dev `useTransition` reference: - **Do not use a transition for a controlled input's value.** The input must update synchronously, or characters appear late or get lost. Split into an urgent state for the input and a transition for the expensive consumer, or use `useDeferredValue`. - **The function passed to `startTransition` runs immediately** and synchronously; React only marks the state updates inside it as transitions. It is not a `setTimeout`. - **Async transitions (React 19).** You can pass an async function, and `isPending` stays true until it settles, which is how Actions and form submissions track pending state. But state updates after an `await` inside it are not automatically marked as transitions in current React; wrap them in another `startTransition` call. - Use the standalone `startTransition` import when you are outside a component (a router or store), at the cost of no `isPending`. ### Transitions vs debounce and throttle | | Debounce | Throttle | Transition / deferred value | |---|---|---|---| | Delay before work starts | Fixed (e.g. 300 ms) | Fixed interval | None: starts immediately | | Fast device | Still waits the full delay | Still waits | Finishes almost instantly | | Slow device | Work may still block the main thread once it starts | Same | Work is interruptible; input stays responsive | | Reduces network requests | Yes | Yes | No | They solve different problems. Use transitions for **expensive rendering**; use debounce for **expensive side effects** such as network calls per keystroke. Often you want both: debounce the fetch, and render the results in a transition. ## useDeferredValue `useDeferredValue(value)` returns a version of the value that "lags behind" during urgent updates: ```tsx function SearchPage() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(''); const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); const isStale = query !== deferredQuery; return ( <> setQuery(e.target.value)} />
{/* must be memoised to benefit */}
); } ``` On each keystroke React first re-renders with the **new** `query` but the **old** `deferredQuery`. If `SlowList` is wrapped in `memo` (or compiled by the React Compiler), it bails out because its prop did not change, so the urgent render is cheap and the input updates immediately. Then React schedules a background re-render with the new deferred value, which is interruptible like a transition. When to use which: - **`useTransition`** when you own the state update (you call the setter). - **`useDeferredValue`** when you receive a value (a prop or a value from a hook you do not control) and want an expensive part of the tree to lag behind it. - React 19 added an `initialValue` argument, `useDeferredValue(value, initialValue)`, so the first render can use a cheap placeholder and then render the real value in the background. ## How it works underneath: lanes and the scheduler React's internals are not public API, but interviewers at strong frontend teams sometimes ask how React decides what to work on. The model is **lanes**: each update is assigned a lane, a bit in a 31-bit mask, and lanes represent priorities. Using bitmasks lets React cheaply group, merge and check sets of pending updates. | Lane (simplified) | Typical source | Behaviour | |---|---|---| | Sync | Discrete events: click, keydown, input | Rendered synchronously, not time-sliced | | Input continuous | Continuous events: mousemove, scroll, pointer drag | High priority | | Default | Updates outside events: network callbacks, timers | Normal priority | | Transition (several lanes) | `startTransition`, `useDeferredValue` background render | Interruptible, time-sliced | | Retry | Re-rendering after a suspended promise resolves | Low | | Idle / Offscreen | Hidden `Activity` content, pre-rendering | Lowest | How a render proceeds: 1. An update is queued on a fiber with a lane chosen from the current context (inside an event handler for a click, the Sync lane; inside `startTransition`, a Transition lane). 2. React marks the path from that fiber to the root as having pending work in that lane, then asks its **scheduler** to process the root. 3. React picks the highest-priority pending lanes and renders only updates in those lanes. Lower-priority updates on the same component are skipped for now and replayed later on top of the new state, so the result is as if all updates applied in order. 4. For time-sliced (concurrent) lanes, the work loop processes one fiber at a time and calls `shouldYield()`. React's scheduler yields roughly every 5 ms, posting a message (via `MessageChannel`) to continue in a new task, so the browser can handle input and paint in between. 5. If a higher-priority update arrives mid-render, React abandons the work-in-progress tree, processes the urgent lane, and later restarts the transition. 6. To avoid **starvation**, lanes that wait too long expire and are processed synchronously. Why it matters for you: - It explains why typing stays responsive during a transition: keystrokes are Sync lane and pre-empt Transition lane work. - It explains why a transition can render a component several times without committing: renders were discarded. Side effects during render would run multiple times, which is why render must be pure. - It explains **tearing** risks with external mutable stores: during an interruptible render, the store could change between rendering two components, which would then show inconsistent values. `useSyncExternalStore` prevents this by forcing a synchronous re-render when the store changes mid-render. ## Practical guidance - Mark navigations and tab switches as transitions (routers already do this) so already-visible content does not flash to a fallback. - Pair transitions with **memoised** expensive children; otherwise the urgent render re-renders them anyway. - Do not wrap everything in transitions. Most updates are fast; transitions add bookkeeping and can make simple state harder to reason about. - Concurrency cannot split a single expensive component. If one component takes 200 ms to render, React cannot yield inside it. Break the work up (virtualise lists, split components) or move computation to a Web Worker. - Measure with the React DevTools Profiler and the React 19.2 performance tracks in Chrome DevTools, which show the Scheduler's priorities alongside the browser's work.

  participant B as Browser

  R->>B: commit input, paint

  R->>R: abandon stale transition render

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Concurrent React questions check three things: that you know concurrency means **interruptible rendering on one thread**, not parallelism; that you can pick the right tool (Suspense, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, or plain debounce); and that you understand the user-visible behaviour: what shows a fallback, what keeps old content, what stays responsive. Senior candidates may be asked how React prioritises work (lanes, the scheduler, yielding) and how this relates to INP.

## Question 1: "What problem does concurrent rendering solve?"

**Model answer:**

> Before React 18, once a render started it ran to completion, so a heavy update like filtering a big list blocked the main thread and the input froze. Concurrent rendering lets React prepare a new UI in the background, yield to the browser every few milliseconds so input and painting can happen, and abandon work that became stale when a newer update arrives. It is safe because rendering is pure and happens on a private work-in-progress tree; only the commit touches the DOM, and that stays synchronous. You opt in per update with transitions, deferred values and Suspense.

## Question 2: "useTransition vs useDeferredValue vs debounce?"

**Model answer:** `useTransition` marks state updates I trigger as non-urgent, giving me `isPending`. `useDeferredValue` is for a value I receive: it renders the tree with the old value first, then catches up in the background; it only helps if the expensive child is memoised. Debounce delays work by a fixed time, which reduces calls, so it fits network requests, but it makes fast devices wait and does not make the work itself interruptible. For a search box I would debounce the request and render results with a transition or deferred value.

## Question 3: "Why does my page flash to a spinner when I switch tabs, and how do you fix it?"

**Model answer:** The tab content suspends on data or code, and because the update is urgent React replaces already-visible content with the nearest Suspense fallback. Wrapping the tab switch in `startTransition` tells React to keep showing the current tab until the new one is ready, and `isPending` lets me dim it or show an inline indicator. Routers do the same for navigations. If I want a fallback for a genuinely new context, such as a new search query, I put a `key` on the boundary.

## Question 4: "How does React decide what to render first?"

**Model answer:** Every update gets a lane, a bit in a bitmask that encodes priority: discrete input like clicks and keystrokes is the sync lane, continuous input like drags is next, normal updates are default, transitions use transition lanes, and hidden or offscreen work is lowest. React renders the highest-priority lanes first, skips lower-priority updates and replays them later so the final state is the same as applying them in order. Concurrent lanes are rendered in time slices: React's scheduler yields about every 5 ms, and if an urgent update arrives it throws away the in-progress render and restarts later. Lanes that wait too long expire and render synchronously, so transitions cannot starve.

## Question 5: "Where should Suspense boundaries go?"

**Model answer:** Each boundary is a unit that appears together, so I place them where a designer would want independent loading: around the main content, around a slow sidebar widget, around comments below the fold. Not around every component, which creates a popcorn effect, and not only at the root, which makes the whole page wait for the slowest part. On the server the same boundaries define streaming and selective hydration, so slow data does not hold back the shell and the user's click prioritises hydrating the region they touched. Fallbacks match the final size to avoid layout shift, and each data region also gets an error boundary.

## Question 6: "Transitions are in place but typing is still janky. Why?"

**Model answer:** Possible causes: the expensive child is not memoised, so the urgent render re-renders it anyway; the controlled input's own value is updated inside the transition, delaying characters; a single component takes 100+ ms to render, and React cannot yield inside one component; or the cost is in the commit (thousands of DOM nodes), which is never interruptible. Fixes: memoise or rely on the compiler, keep the input state urgent, split or virtualise the list, and move heavy computation to a Web Worker. I would confirm with the Profiler and a Performance panel recording of the interaction.

## Code question

```tsx
function App() {
  const [tab, setTab] = useState('home');
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setTab('photos')}>Photos</button>
      <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
        {tab === 'home' ? <Home /> : <Photos />}  {/* Photos suspends for 1 s */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}
```

"What does the user see after clicking, and how would you change it?" **Answer:** The Home content disappears and the spinner shows for a second, then Photos appears. Wrapping `setTab` in `startTransition` keeps Home visible (optionally dimmed using `isPending`) until Photos is ready, which feels faster and avoids the flash.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Is concurrent rendering multi-threaded?" | No. One main thread; React interleaves and abandons render work |
| "Can a commit be interrupted?" | No. Only the render phase is interruptible |
| "Why must renders be pure for this to work?" | React may render a tree several times and discard results; side effects would run each time |
| "What is tearing?" | Components showing different values of the same external store in one commit; `useSyncExternalStore` prevents it |
| "Does useEffect fetching trigger Suspense?" | No. Suspense needs the component to suspend during render (lazy, `use`, a Suspense-enabled library) |
| "What is selective hydration?" | Boundaries hydrate independently; React prioritises the one the user interacts with |
| "What is Activity for?" | Hide UI while keeping state, with hidden updates at lowest priority and effects cleaned up |

## Common mistakes

- Describing transitions as "a setTimeout" or "debounce built in".
- Putting the controlled input's value inside `startTransition`.
- Forgetting that `useDeferredValue` needs a memoised consumer to help.
- Wrapping every component in Suspense, or only the root.
- Creating promises during a client render and passing them to `use`, causing infinite suspension loops.
- Claiming concurrency fixes slow single components or slow commits.

keyPoints: Concurrent rendering is interruptible rendering on one thread; it is safe because render is pure and only the commit touches the DOM.
Suspense shows the nearest fallback when a child suspends on lazy code, use(promise) or a Suspense-enabled library; effects-based fetching does not suspend.
Each Suspense boundary is a unit that appears together, and on the server it defines streaming and selective hydration.
Transitions keep already-visible content instead of flashing a fallback, expose isPending, and are discarded when stale.
useDeferredValue renders with the old value first and catches up in the background; it needs a memoised expensive child.
Lanes are bitmask priorities: discrete input pre-empts transitions, React yields about every 5 ms, and starved lanes expire to sync.
Concurrency cannot split one slow component or a large commit; virtualise, split components or use a worker.

check.q: A user switches tabs and the new tab suspends on data. With a plain setState, the old tab is replaced by a spinner. What does wrapping the update in startTransition change?
options: The data loads faster
React keeps showing the old tab until the new one is ready, and isPending is true meanwhile
React skips the Suspense boundary and renders the tab without data
The tab switch runs in a Web Worker
check.why: Updates in a transition do not replace already-visible content with a fallback. React keeps the current UI and exposes isPending so you can show an inline indicator.

check.q: You use useDeferredValue(query) and pass the deferred value to a large list, but typing is still slow. What is the most likely cause?
options: The list component is not memoised, so it re-renders during the urgent render anyway
useDeferredValue only works in Server Components
useDeferredValue adds a fixed 300 ms delay
The input should be uncontrolled for deferred values to work
check.why: The urgent render passes the old deferred value; a memoised child bails out because its prop is unchanged. Without memo (or the compiler), it re-renders on every keystroke.

check.q: Which statement about React's lanes and scheduler is accurate?
options: Transitions run on a separate thread
All updates have equal priority and are processed in order
The commit phase is time-sliced so the browser can paint between DOM mutations
Discrete input updates pre-empt transition renders, which yield roughly every 5 ms and restart when stale
check.why: Updates get lanes by priority. Concurrent lanes render in short time slices and are abandoned if more urgent work arrives. Commit is always synchronous, and everything runs on the main thread.
